## Phase V — The Easter Offensive and Linebacker (Jan 1972 – Dec 1972)

### How the phase ends (changed)

At the end of 1972 the war is on the verge of a settlement that both governments in Vietnam regard as provisional. The Easter Offensive has failed to destroy the ARVN or the Thieu government, at a cost to the PAVN of most of the armour it committed (by one count 134 T-54s, 56 PT-76s and 60 T-34s) and, on the historical count, about 100,000 men. The ARVN has held at An Loc and Kontum and retaken Quang Tri City, but has lost Quang Tri north of the Thach Han, the western Highlands and the border areas of III Corps, and its losses are given variously from about 10,000 killed to about 39,000 dead in the period. Almost a million South Vietnamese have been made refugees, about 600,000 of them in government camps¹.

In this war the PAVN's losses for the year are higher than that count, and higher in particular formations. The GBU-38 cells added perhaps a fifth to the losses of the B-2 Front's divisions around An Loc, the siege box destroyed about a third of the guns brought to Kontum before the assault and broke the 320th Division's assault short of the wire, and the radar-bombing of the armour on the DMZ destroyed some 20–30 vehicles before they reached the firebases². Taken together I put the PAVN's killed and wounded in 1972 at about 7,000–10,000 above the historical figure, roughly a tenth more, concentrated in the 5th, 7th and 9th Divisions and the 320th and 2nd Divisions, which are the formations that will fight Phuoc Long, Ban Me Thuot and Xuan Loc. The North replaces that difference within its flow of men for 1973³. What it does not replace as quickly is the experienced cadre killed in the measured assaults, and the 7th and 9th Divisions enter 1974 with greener companies than history's⁴.

The countryside ends 1972 in two parts. Where a PAVN division came into the peopled lowlands, in northern Binh Dinh and Quang Tri, the gains of 1964–71 were lost and the hamlets returned to the state history left them in. In the held belt of the Delta and around Saigon the posts held through the year, the Front's infrastructure inside the post line did not return, and the files that will open the "war of the flags" survived intact. In Saigon the decree powers and the end of the hamlet elections took back the government's claim to the hamlets' consent, as they did historically. The historical land programme has by now distributed about a million hectares of its own, and the margin of the 1964 titling over history has narrowed to its six years of head start and the councils that confirmed it. Night control and the Front's weakness in the held belt remain one band better than history's; the government's legitimacy has returned to history's; and the Special Branch's knowledge of the infrastructure, which the historical police and Phoenix had largely caught up with by 1972, is one band better rather than two⁴.

The lesson both sides draw is the same. The ARVN held where American air power was decisive, at An Loc and Kontum, and where American advisers coordinated it; it broke where its leadership failed, at Quang Tri and Tan Canh. The settlement about to be signed removes the American advisers and the American air power and leaves the PAVN in the South, while the North's air defences and economy recover. Hanoi needs only to rebuild, wait for the Americans to be gone, and choose its time.

The aircraft are still flying at the end of 1972, still American, and under the agreement about to be signed they will soon have no American strike force to cue. The Republic keeps nothing of them: no aircraft, no exploitation cells, no practice in using either.

The ARVN has held An Loc and Kontum more cheaply than history's, and has learned more completely that it holds besieged towns with American bombers measured onto the enemy by American analysts. The agreement about to be signed takes both away. The Republic enters 1973 more confident than history's and more dependent².

The ARVN's regiments and battalions have fought the offensive better than history's, and its divisions and corps no better: Quang Tri was lost by orders, and the column on Highway 1 was saved in part by a regiment. It has learned, from An Loc and Kontum, to use American air with an educated staff's precision, and it has no air of its own that its plans can rest on⁵.

### New: The northern districts of Binh Dinh
*Apr – Aug 1972 · Hoai Nhon, Tam Quan and Hoai An districts, Binh Dinh Province · EVMT01-1*

*Initiative: enemy*

While the world watched Quang Tri, Kontum and An Loc, the PAVN 3rd Division, the Yellow Star, came down out of the An Lao valley in April 1972 and took the three northern districts of Binh Dinh, Hoai Nhon, Tam Quan and Hoai An, from the 22nd Division's 40th and 41st Regiments and the province's Regional Forces; the district towns and the old American base at Landing Zone English were in its hands by the end of the month, and the districts were retaken over the summer. It was the only place in 1972 where the offensive reached a densely peopled coastal lowland and held it for months, and it is the one place where the record can see what the offensive did to the countryside the provisions had built.

What it did was not what it did historically, and it ended in the same place. In 1964 the land programme had titled the rice land of the Bong Son plain to the men who tilled it, much of it land the Viet Minh had given them first⁶. When the Front's district committee came back behind the Yellow Star in late April, it had nothing to give. Its cadres held meetings in Tam Quan in May at which, by the account of a district cadre captured in August, the peasants asked whether the Front would confirm their titles, and the cadre had no instruction to answer. So it governed the three districts as an occupying administration rather than a revolution: it taxed the spring harvest at the rate its own documents set for "liberated zones under enemy pressure", took about 1,800 young men for its local battalions, and executed or took away the hamlet chiefs and police it could find. The district Special Branch office at Bong Son had burned its files on 22 April, three hours before the town fell, on the order of the district chief, Major Dao Van Luong, who had served in the province since 1966 and had seen what Hue cost⁴.

The return of the 22nd Division and the Regional Forces in July and August found hamlets that had paid more to the Front in four months than in the eight years before, and fewer young men in them; about 70,000 people from the three districts had gone south to the camps at Phu My and Qui Nhon and most did not come back before 1973⁴. The night in northern Binh Dinh went back to where it had been on the historical course, and the government that returned was the one that had left. The province's gains of 1964–71 were lost here not because the land reform failed, but because the offensive put a PAVN division in the hamlets for four months and the posts had no answer to a division. That is the mechanism by which the coastal lowlands converged with history in 1972, and it reached only where a division went.

### New: The Delta during the offensive
*Apr – Oct 1972 · Chuong Thien and Kien Giang provinces; the U Minh forest · EVMT01-2*

*Initiative: enemy*

When the 21st Division left the Delta in April 1972 to fight its way up Route 13 toward An Loc, the regiments the PAVN and the Front had kept in the U Minh forest came out against the outposts of Chuong Thien and Kien Giang. Historically this is where the offensive reached the Delta's countryside: dozens of posts lost, districts cut off, and the government's figures for its own security falling for the first time since 1968. In this war the posts were different. The Popular Forces platoons of Long My and Kien Thien districts had held their posts beside the police since 1964, with the land titled behind them, and the attacks of April and May fell on posts that held about nine attacks in ten⁷. The Front's regiments therefore did what they did everywhere else in this war: they left the held posts alone and went for the Regional Force companies the province chiefs had been made to send north as convoy escorts for the 21st Division's resupply, and for the road.

Major Huynh Cong Tri, the district chief of Long My, a list chief since 1966, kept every one of his forty-one posts through the summer and lost the road to Vi Thanh for seven weeks. His monthly reports, which CORDS forwarded to the Joint General Staff in September as the model of a district under siege, say that the Front's tax collectors did not come into the hamlets inside the post line between April and October, and collected in the hamlets outside it at about twice their 1971 rate. The same was true across the western Delta. The held belt stayed held at night through the worst year since 1968, and the contested belt beyond it, which the offensive gave back to the Front for a season, was where the Front's tax take and recruitment recovered⁴. By October the 21st Division was back and the roads were open.

This is the half of the Phase IV gain that survived 1972. The Front's infrastructure inside the post line did not return in 1972, because the offensive in the Delta came as regiments against the posts and not as cadres into the hamlets; and the files of the district centres, which the attacks never reached, are the files with which the IV Corps provinces opened the "war of the flags" in January 1973. Night control in the held belt and the Front's weakness there were still one band better than history's at the end of 1972; what returned to history was the contested belt, the coast where a division came, and the government's legitimacy, which was lost in Saigon.

### New: The decree powers and the end of the hamlet elections
*Jun – Sep 1972 · Saigon · EVMT01-3*

*Initiative: allied*

At the end of June 1972, with the offensive still on three fronts, the Senate gave President Thieu power to rule by decree for six months on matters of defence, security and the economy, and he used it. A press decree of August 1972 required newspapers to post a bond that closed most of the opposition press within weeks, and in the late summer of 1972 the election of hamlet chiefs, introduced in 1967, was abolished and the chiefs were appointed through the province and district chiefs. It was the largest step back from the Republic's own constitution since 1967, and it was taken for the palace's reasons, not the enemy's: the President was preparing for the ceasefire that the Americans were negotiating over his head, and wanted every hamlet chief in the country to be his own man when the flags went up.

In this war the decree fell on a countryside where elected hamlet chiefs mattered more than they had historically, because they sat on the councils that had confirmed the land titles of 1964 and heard the disputes over them⁶. The province and district chiefs who appointed their successors were, since 1970, the palace's choices from the Board's list, and in the Delta many of them replaced the elected chief with the same man; elsewhere, in the coastal provinces and in II Corps, they did not. The government's standing in the hamlets fell to where it stood on the historical course, for the historical reason, and with one difference that history did not have: in the hamlets where land had been titled under elected councils, the appointed chiefs were the men who could now hear the land disputes, and the Front's district committees made that their whole propaganda for the ceasefire⁴.

The net of this event is not a gain undone. The land titles, the posts and the files of the held belt were untouched by the decree; what it took was the one thing in the countryside that had made the government's arrival a matter of the hamlet's own choosing. That loss is history's, the gain beneath it is this war's, and the two together leave the Republic at the end of 1972 holding more of its countryside at night than the historical Republic held, on a narrower claim to the hamlets' consent⁴.

## Phase VI — Paris, the endgame, and 1975 (Jan 1973 – Dec 1975)

### How the phase ends (changed)

The war ends on 30 April 1975 with the fall of Saigon and the unconditional surrender of the Republic of Vietnam. In this war that date is a conclusion and not an assumption: it was set in Hanoi by a resolution to finish before the rains and by the march of the 1st Corps, and the mechanisms in this war that pulled the fall later (the better battalions at Duc Duc, Xuan Loc, Phan Rang and Cu Chi, the PAVN's greener divisions, a stronger held belt in the Delta) acted on fights the PAVN chose to bypass, while those that pulled it earlier (a President more certain his army could not hold alone, an army more dependent on fire it no longer had) acted on decisions the palace took on the historical days for its own reasons⁴. Rung (a), collapse. The Paris Agreement had removed the American forces and kept the PAVN in the South; Congress had written the end of American combat and the limits on the President into law; American military aid had fallen; and the government in Saigon, more stable than at any time since 1963 but narrowly based, economically weakened and dependent on American supply, faced an enemy that had rebuilt after 1972 and chose its moment. The decisive blows were Hanoi's, at Phuoc Long and Ban Me Thuot; the decisive errors were Saigon's, in the order to abandon the Highlands and the contradictory orders to I Corps.

The Republic that met the offensive was not the historical Republic, and the end vector of this phase, measured after the fall, cannot show it. At the end of 1974, on the eve of Phuoc Long, the held belt of the Delta and the Saigon region was held at night more firmly than history's, and the Front's district committees there had lost about twice the historical share of their members in 1973⁸; the Special Branch's knowledge of the infrastructure was still the better for its ten years of files; the government's standing in the hamlets was history's, after the decrees of 1972; the army's battalions were better led and its divisions and corps no better; and the army as a whole was more dependent than history's on American fire it no longer had, and knew it⁴. Every one of those differences was erased by the fall, and the vector returns to history because the state it measured no longer existed.

Hanoi's posture never changed. It was committed to armed reunification throughout, from the Ninth Plenum of December 1963 to the Ho Chi Minh Campaign, through the losses of 1965–68 and 1972, and it accepted the Paris Agreement as a step towards that end. The timing of its last campaign was its own, set by its army's road and the season. The US war in Vietnam, from the advisory years to 1973, cost more than 58,000 American dead. The Vietnamese dead, military and civilian, northern and southern, are counted in the millions by most estimates, and the record of them is less precise than the record of the Americans.

The squad guns and the marksmen's rifles of the ARVN, and about 9 million rounds of linked 5.56mm from the divisional hoards of I and II Corps, are in the PAVN's hands by the end of April 1975, with the carbines of a million men⁹.

The Republic's defence of every besieged town had been built since 1971 around American bombers and American coordinates, and both were gone by the end of 1973².

The officers the reforms made fought the last campaign as well as any part of the RVNAF fought it, and their best staff plan was taken by the President and executed without its method. About 12,000 of the board's officers were captured in 1975 and sent to the re-education camps with the rest of the officer corps; the board's files, with the evaluation report of every officer since 1964, were in the Joint General Staff's compound on 30 April⁵.

### Changed: Resolution 21 and the North's rebuilding
*Oct 1973 – 1974 · Hanoi; the Laotian panhandle and the western Highlands · EV000-87*

*Initiative: enemy*

In October 1973 the 21st Plenum of the Party Central Committee in Hanoi resolved that the revolution in the South must continue by the path of revolutionary violence, and that the PAVN should respond to Saigon's operations and prepare for a decisive offensive. The PAVN rebuilt through 1973 and 1974: it improved the strategic road along the western side of South Vietnam east of the Truong Son, extended the fuel pipeline into the South, built up stocks of ammunition and armour in the base areas and grouped its divisions into army corps, the 1st Corps in October 1973 and the 4th Corps on 20 July 1974 among them¹⁰. It was the North's own decision, on its own reading of the American political collapse and Saigon's weakness, and it was taken while Saigon still held the initiative in the countryside.

In this war the rebuilding had about a tenth more to make good from 1972, most of it in the divisions that had been struck at An Loc and Kontum. It made it good on the historical schedule, and the schedule is the point. The corps were formed on their historical dates because what governed them was the Politburo's decision of October 1973 and the American political collapse it was reading, not the number of men in the B-2 Front's regiments; the North's flow of replacements to the South in 1973 covered the difference in men within a season, and the B-2 Front's command filled the 7th and 9th Divisions' companies with new conscripts under the surviving cadre. What the difference bought was quality, not time: the 9th Division that attacked Rach Bap in May 1974 and the 7th that went into Phuoc Long in December had fewer company commanders who had fought in 1972 than history's, and their first assaults in each battle were cruder⁴. The PAVN's losses of 1972 therefore left the date of every 1974 and 1975 operation where history put it, and made a few of them dearer.

It was the North's own decision, on its own reading of the American political collapse and Saigon's weakness, and it was taken while Saigon still held the initiative in the countryside.

### Changed: The collapse of I Corps
*13–30 Mar 1975 · Quang Tri, Hue and Da Nang · EV000-94*

*Initiative: enemy*
On 13 March Thieu ordered Truong to give up most of I Corps and withdrew the Airborne Division towards Saigon as a reserve. On 20 March he ordered Truong to hold only Da Nang; on 29 March he ordered him to turn back and retake it, which Truong refused. The contradictory orders, given as the PAVN 2nd Corps with the 304th, 324th and 325th Divisions attacked from the north and west and the 2nd Division and 52nd Brigade struck in Quang Ngai and Quang Tin, broke I Corps. Northern Quang Tri was lost by 18 March; Hue was surrounded by the evening of 25 March and abandoned; about 6,000 soldiers of the 2nd Division deserted on 28 March; and the PAVN entered Da Nang on the afternoon of 29 March. Soldiers abandoned their units to find their families, and the sea evacuation from Da Nang became chaos, with people fighting to board the ships. I Corps had about 134,000 men against more than 75,000 PAVN and VC; three ARVN infantry divisions and the 147th Marine Brigade ceased to exist, and about 58,722 soldiers were captured at Hue. The PAVN took 129 aircraft, 179 armoured vehicles and 327 artillery pieces¹¹. The best corps in the ARVN, under its best commander, had been destroyed without a decisive battle.

In this war the battalions that had held their companies together at Duc Duc in 1974 went to pieces in March 1975 as history's did, and the reason is the one thing the reforms never touched: the soldiers' families. The ARVN soldier's wife and children lived in the dependants' quarters beside his unit's base or in the town behind it, because his pay, worth a fraction of its 1971 value after the inflation of 1973–74, could not keep two households. In 1974 the battalions fought on ridges with their families safe behind them; in March 1975 the order to give up the north put the families in the path of the PAVN, and the men went to them. A board-chosen battalion commander can hold a company under fire, and the 3rd Division's commanders held theirs at Duc Duc; no commander, chosen by anyone, holds a man whose children are on the road to Da Nang with the PAVN behind them⁴. What absorbed the difference the officer reforms had made was an order from the palace that turned a corps into a column of families.

In this war the PAVN's security troops who entered Da Nang on 29 March went first, by a list prepared in Hanoi, to the I Corps regional office of the Special Branch and the Quang Nam PIOCC. The destruction plan of 1968 had been rehearsed every quarter for seven years; on 28 March the regional chief, who had sent his family to the docks that morning, did not order it, and the clerks who might have done it on their own had gone to find theirs. The Quang Tri and Thua Thien centres had burned their files on the 18th and 25th; Quang Nam, Quang Tin and Quang Ngai did not, and the regional office held district extracts of the national file for all five provinces with about 40,000 names and about 11,000 photographs⁸. That the collapse would deliver the files with the corps was the risk the memorandum that created them had named.

### New: The Politburo's calendar: Saigon before the rains
*25 Mar – 14 Apr 1975 · Hanoi and the roads south · EVMT01-4*

*Initiative: enemy*

The date of the fall of Saigon was set in Hanoi between 25 March and 14 April, and it was set by the rains and by the road. On 25 March, with Hue abandoned and the Highlands column destroyed, the Politburo resolved to take Saigon before the rainy season, which in the southern provinces begins in May and turns the lowlands around the capital to mud; on 31 March, with Da Nang taken, it decided to do it in April; and on 14 April it named the operation the Ho Chi Minh Campaign. Between those dates the whole of the PAVN's effort went into moving its corps to the capital: the 1st Corps, the strategic reserve, was brought south from the North by road, a march of more than 1,500 kilometres, and reached its assembly areas north of Saigon only in the third week of April; the 2nd Corps came down the coast behind the collapse of I and II Corps; and the 3rd and 4th Corps closed from the Highlands and the east¹². General Van Tien Dung's plan set the assault for the last days of April because that was when the last corps would be in place and the first rains still a fortnight off.

In this war the inputs to that plan were different in three places and the plan was not. Dung's staff knew from the prisoners of Duc Duc and the reports of 1974 that the ARVN's battalions were better led than in 1972, and from the first three days at Xuan Loc that the 18th Division's squads could stop an assault battalion at 400 metres. It drew the conclusion it had drawn at every stage of the war, and it drew it faster: a well-led ARVN division is to be bypassed and isolated, not assaulted, and the assault is kept for the moment when the defence has nothing behind it. In the Delta the Front was weaker than history's, and Group 232's task of cutting Route 4 to the south of the capital fell more to PAVN regiments and less to the Front's local forces; it was done on the historical day. And the 7th and 9th Divisions, with the green companies of 1972's losses, were given the roles in which greenness cost least⁴.

None of the three reached the critical path. The date of 30 April was the product of the march of the 1st Corps and of a resolution to finish before the rains, and nothing the reforms had built in the ARVN stood on the road from Thanh Hoa to Binh Duong. A delay of a few days at Xuan Loc or Phan Rang was absorbed by a plan that was waiting for its last corps anyway; only a delay of about three weeks or more in the collapse of I and II Corps, enough to keep the 1st Corps' road or the coast closed into May, would have put the assault into the rains and forced Hanoi to choose between fighting in the mud and waiting for the dry season of 1976⁴. That delay was in the hands of the President who gave the orders of 13 and 14 March, and of nobody the reforms had chosen.

### Changed: Xuan Loc
*9–21 Apr 1975 · Xuan Loc, Long Khanh Province, northeast of Saigon · EV000-96*

*Initiative: enemy*

On 9 April the PAVN 4th Corps under Major General Hoang Cam, with the 6th, 7th and 341st Divisions and tanks and artillery, attacked Xuan Loc, the road junction northeast of Saigon on Route 1. The town was held by the ARVN 18th Division under Brigadier General Le Minh Dao, with the 1st Airborne Brigade, armoured units, Rangers and Regional Forces, and air support from Bien Hoa and Tan Son Nhut. The 18th Division held for twelve days against repeated assaults; on 12 April two BLU-82 bombs were dropped on PAVN troops, reportedly killing about 200¹³.

In this war the 18th Division fought at Xuan Loc with what was left of a decade's equipment and, by April, with the ammunition the Joint General Staff could send it from the Long Binh depot, which by then was most of what remained in III Corps. Its squads had their squad guns and the belts to feed them for the first time since January 1974, because Dao drew everything Long Binh would give him; its marksmen held the edges of the town against the 341st Division's infantry crossing the rubber and the open ground east of the town on 9–11 April, and the 43rd Regiment's account of the first three days records the PAVN assault battalions going to ground at 400 metres under fire they could not locate. The ammunition that might have let it hold longer had gone in March, in the divisional hoards at Hue, Da Nang and Qui Nhon that were abandoned when I Corps and the coast collapsed: about 9 million rounds of linked 5.56mm and most of the match 7.62mm in the country, captured intact⁹.

The better fight changed the PAVN's method sooner and did not change the day the town was given up. Historically Hoang Cam's assaults of 9–14 April failed, and he changed his approach after a week: he turned on the 1st Airborne Brigade and the guns at Dau Giay, isolated the town and shelled Bien Hoa's airfield, and on 19 April the Joint General Staff ordered the withdrawal. Here the assaults of 9–11 April were broken more expensively, and on the evening of 11 April, three days earlier than history's turn, Dung's headquarters told Cam to stop assaulting the town and cut it off; Cam's 6th Division went round to Dau Giay and Route 1 west of the town on 12–13 April⁴. The town was then held, as it was historically, by a division that the PAVN no longer needed to take, until the Joint General Staff withdrew it on 19–21 April to defend Bien Hoa and the capital. What absorbed the difference was the enemy's choice to bypass, and behind it a calendar that wanted the 4th Corps at the gates of Saigon on the day the 1st Corps arrived, not on the day Xuan Loc fell. The 3rd Battalion of the 1st Airborne Brigade was destroyed in the withdrawal at Suoi Ca¹³.

The PAVN claimed 2,036 ARVN killed or wounded and 2,731 captured and admitted 460 killed and 1,428 wounded; Americans estimated about 5,000 PAVN casualties and 37 tanks destroyed¹³. I keep the reported figures, which already disagree by a factor of about three, and judge that the PAVN's loss in the three days of assault was perhaps a fifth higher than history's, after which it stopped paying it⁴. On 17 April Phnom Penh fell to the Khmer Rouge.

The 18th Division's battalions at Xuan Loc were commanded by officers the board had chosen and its regiments by colonels it had promoted, and Dao himself had been one of the list's names in 1972⁵. Elsewhere in April the same kind of fight met the same answer. The 22nd Division had come out of Qui Nhon by sea at the beginning of the month, with more of its battalions in being than history's, and was refitted and put into the line south of the capital at Tan An on Route 4, where it was still fighting on 30 April. At Phan Rang the 2nd Airborne Brigade and the territorials held the airbase until 16 April, when the 2nd Corps' columns came down Route 1 in a strength nothing could hold, and Lieutenant General Nguyen Vinh Nghi was taken there. West of Saigon the 25th Division under Brigadier General Ly Tong Ba, who had held Kontum in 1972, kept Cu Chi and Route 1 toward Trang Bang until the last days of April, when the 3rd Corps came on it with more divisions than it had regiments. None of them changed the date, and not because they fought no better than history's: they were fights the PAVN chose to go round, or to take with a weight it was bringing to Saigon anyway, on a schedule set in Hanoi by the rains⁴.

**Before:**

> *Initiative: enemy*
> 
> On 9 April the PAVN 4th Corps under Major General Hoang Cam, with the 6th, 7th and 341st Divisions and tanks and artillery, attacked Xuan Loc, the road junction northeast of Saigon on Route 1. The town was held by the ARVN 18th Division under Brigadier General Le Minh Dao, with the 1st Airborne Brigade, armoured units, Rangers and Regional Forces, and air support from Bien Hoa and Tan Son Nhut. The 18th Division held for twelve days against repeated assaults; on 12 April two BLU-82 bombs were dropped on PAVN troops, reportedly killing about 200.
> 
> In this war the 18th Division fought at Xuan Loc with what was left of a decade's equipment and, by April, with the ammunition the Joint General Staff could send it from the Long Binh depot, which by then was most of what remained in III Corps. Its squads had their squad guns and the belts to feed them for the first time since January 1974, because Dao drew everything Long Binh would give him; its marksmen held the edges of the town against the 341st Division's infantry crossing the rubber and the open ground east of the town on 9–11 April, and the 43rd Regiment's account of the first three days records the PAVN assault battalions going to ground at 400 metres under fire they could not locate. It held for twelve days, as it held historically. The ammunition that might have let it hold longer had gone in March, in the divisional hoards at Hue, Da Nang and Qui Nhon that were abandoned when I Corps and the coast collapsed: about 9 million rounds of linked 5.56mm and most of the match 7.62mm in the country, captured intact.
> 
> The PAVN changed its approach, bypassed and isolated the town, and on 19 April the Joint General Staff ordered the withdrawal; Xuan Loc was abandoned on 21 April, and the 3rd Battalion of the 1st Airborne Brigade was destroyed in the withdrawal at Suoi Ca. The PAVN claimed 2,036 ARVN killed or wounded and 2,731 captured and admitted 460 killed and 1,428 wounded; Americans estimated about 5,000 PAVN casualties and 37 tanks destroyed. I do not adjust these figures; the squad weapons raised the price of each assault and the PAVN answered, as it did historically, by not making more of them⁹. On 17 April Phnom Penh fell to the Khmer Rouge. Xuan Loc was the ARVN's last stand, and showed what a well-led division could still do; it bought twelve days.
> 
> The 18th Division's battalions at Xuan Loc were commanded by officers the board had chosen and its regiments by colonels it had promoted, and Dao himself had been one of the list's names in 1972. In this war there were more divisions like it: the 22nd's stand on the coast in late March, the Airborne brigades at Phan Rang, and the 25th Division's battalions on Route 1 west of Saigon fought in the same way, and none of them changed the arithmetic of 1975, because the corps above them had already gone⁵. Xuan Loc held for twelve days, as it did historically¹³.
